narrative:
The model estimates a 48% chance that you will leave your current role, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution against investing in someone who might soon depart.

Three factors stood out most in the model’s reasoning. First, the fact that you have received other job opportunities while working here pushed the prediction strongly toward leaving. Employees predicted to stay rarely report receiving such external offers, so this signal carried the heaviest weight. Second, your six-to-ten years of experience in your current organization pulled the prediction back toward staying. Most employees the model expects to remain have shorter tenure in their present role, making your length of service a meaningful stabilizing factor. Third, your overall career experience of six-to-ten years also nudged the outcome slightly toward leaving. While many who stay have even less total experience, your mid-range profile still contributed a modest push away from long-term retention.

Taken together, the external opportunities outweighed the retention value of your tenure, tipping the balance just enough for the system to forecast departure.

The organization should discuss with you how to reduce the appeal of outside offers, perhaps through clearer promotion paths or improved recognition. You may wish to reflect on whether your current rewards, training access, and sense of appreciation truly match your expectations. Addressing these points could strengthen your commitment and open future promotion opportunities. (248 words)
